lectures.title: Understanding The Data Cache & Cache Settings

memoization feature.

after this one initial request, if I reload

and come back, no further requests are
sent to the backend.
As you can tell by the fact that no new
logs are being added here.
At least that will be the case if you are
using Next.js version 14.
And as mentioned before, you can check
your package.json file to find out which
version you are using.
If you are on Next.js version 15 or higher,
you actually will see multiple requests
here because the default caching
behavior of fetch requests, so of requests
sent with the fetch function as we are
doing it here, has been changed with
Next.js version 15.
Now I'll get back to that and for the
moment, I'll assume you are using
Next.js version 14 or older, and I'll walk
you through the behavior there before
I'll then get back to the Next.js version 15
behavior.
No matter how often I reload this page
or navigate back and forth, no new logs
are added.
And that's the case because of this data
cache that's also provided by Next.js.
Because what Next.js does when using
the fetch function for fetching data from
a backend is it will store the response
data fetched from there in some
internally managed server-side cache
and it will keep reusing that data forever
until you tell it to not do that anymore.
Now, how can you tell Next.js to not
reuse that data anymore?
Well, you could call revalidatePath as you
learned before in this course after you
changed some data, but here I'm not
actually changing the data on that
dummy backend, so I won't do that here,

the previous section already because
that would tell Next.js that the data for a
specific path, so the data used on a
specific page, did change and it would
throw away the respective data cache.
But alternatively, you can also configure
this fetch function because you can add
a configuration object to it and on that
configuration object, you can set various
settings.
For example, the cache setting.
You can do that when using fetch in the
browser side and you can also do that
when using fetch on the server side.
Now, what's important to understand
here is that on the server side, Next.js is
actually overriding the default built-in
function that is provided by modern
Node.js and it essentially does that so
that it can find out what cache settings
you set up here because that will then
change the behavior of the Next.js
cache.
And here, you get various options,
though the two important options when
using Next.js are force cache, which is
the default with Next.js version 14, which
gives you the most aggressive caching
behavior as this setting, force cache, will
ensure that the response yielded for this
fetch request will be cached and reused
across requests until you give Next.js an
indication that the fetched data has
changed.
So that's the aggressive default behavior
you get with Next.js 14.
The other important setting is no store,
which is the default with Next.js 15 or
higher, which is why you see multiple
requests hitting the backend if you are
using Next.js 15 or later because with no
store, Next.js will not store the response
yielded by the fetch request.
It will not cache it.
So you don't have that aggressive
caching behavior there.
Of course, you could switch to force
cache if you wanted, if you want more
efficiency, if you want more caching, but
the default with Next.js 15 is no store.
The other options, at least at the point of
time where I'm recording this, are not
important for the Next.js cache
management.
But cache no store will tell Next.js that
for this fetch request in this place, so not
in other places where the same request
is sent, but instead just in this place, the
data should not be cached.
Instead, now with this setting, I'm
forcing Next.js to always send a new

that request instead of caching and
reusing the data.
And therefore, if I save that, I can already
see that some new logs were added
here.
The number may vary for you, but if I
reload the messages app a couple of

So that's this no store setting.

API if using it in a Next.js application,

wants an object, which allows me to set
a revalidate setting.
And here I can define a number, which

So if I set this to five, I'm telling Next.js

And then thereafter, it should throw

And within that five second timeframe, if

If I reload this page, I got one request

And of course that five second

used.
So setting this revalidate setting is an
elegant way of ensuring that you get
some caching advantages, but you're
not caching data forever.
So you can control caching
with help of those fetch function settings.
You can alternatively
also add some file-wide settings
in case you had multiple components in that file
that would maybe all send fetch requests.
Instead of then configuring
all those requests manually step by step,
you could set up a configuration for the entire file,
which would then be used for all the requests
sent from anywhere in that file.
And you do that with help of two special constants
you can add to your NextJS files.
The first constant is the revalidate constant.
This constant serves the same purpose

I showed you a couple of seconds ago.
You can set it to a number
and that will be the number of seconds
for which data will be cached and reused
until a new request will be sent.
Now for NextJS to pick up that constant,
you also must export it,

So with that added,
even if I don't set it on the fetch function,
I'll get this same behavior as before.
I got some logs here
and now if I hammer the refresh button,

you see only one new request was sent to the backend

So that's one way of setting this up file-wide.
Now you can also set up that other setting

Because you can also export a constant called dynamic,

This dynamic constant takes various values.
The default is auto and doesn't have to be set.
Alternatively, you can set this to force dynamic,

as if you set the cache setting on a fetch request
to no store.
Because force dynamic tells NextJS
to always re-fetch all the data
that's needed anywhere in that file,
which is exactly the same
this cache no store setting did,
now just applied to all requests
sent from anywhere in that file.
With that setting added,
if I open that backend log again

You could also set this to force static to force caching,

But force dynamic would be another way

It's not what I'll do here,

And then, there is one last way of making sure

That's what unstable no store does.
And therefore here again, if I restart that backend server

or refresh shortcut,
you see a bunch of logs here

So that's another function in this case you should know.

lectures.title: Making Sense Of The Full Route Cache

cues.en: So we did now learn
about a lot of different cache settings,
and we learned how those settings can be used
to control the data cache.
Now, besides that data cache,
NextJS also has a full route cache,
and that's actually the kind of cache
we saw in action in this application before.
Because that full route cache is actually already created
and initialized at build time,
which simply means that if I stop that development server
and I build this NextJS application for production
by running npm run build, NextJS goes ahead
and pre-renders all the pages of this application,
unless they're dynamic pages with a dynamic parameter,
because there, by default,
it doesn't know all the possible dynamic parameter values,
but it pre-renders all the pages it's able to pre-render.
You also see that here, that all those pages marked
with a dot were pre-rendered,
so the messages page, for example,
was pre-rendered, as you can tell,
and the implication of that is
that when we start the production server with npm start,
it will actually be those pre-rendered pages
that we see out of the box, and those pages
are actually cached by NextJS, you could say.
Therefore, now with that production server up and running,
if I clear and restart my backend,
we will actually see no log message at all here
when I reload that messages page,
and we see no log message here at all
because that page was pre-rendered at build time
and it's cached, and it's now always
that pre-rendered cached page that's being served here,
no matter how often I reload or navigate away and come back.
It's always that pre-rendered page.
Hence, we got no logs here on that backend server.
Now, that's, of course, fine,
as long as the data here doesn't change,
and in this dummy application with that dummy backend,
that's the case because the data served
from that dummy backend does never change,
but we saw before in the previous section
where we learned about data mutations with NextJS
that this can be a problem if we have data that does change,
because due to that pre-rendered cached page,
NextJS never re-renders and updates that page,
And that's another thing that will be controlled
by setting one of these cache settings here.
For example, if I set force dynamic to this entire file
to make sure that there is no data caching,
I automatically also disable the full route cache
for this page, and I make sure that,
instead of pre-rendering and caching this page,
NextJS will always re-render that page
whenever a request is sent to it,
which ensures that we're always fetching fresh data,
and that's why, when I enable this dynamic constant
and set it to force dynamic here, and I then save that file,
and I then rebuild my project to rebuild it for production,
now, this messages route has a different symbol here,
which means that it's a dynamic page now,
which is server-rendered on demand,
as you can tell down here.
And indeed, that's what we can see
when we start the production server with npm start.
Now, if we take a look at this backend log,
if I reload this page a couple of times,
I see a bunch of logs here,
because now it's not just the data cache that's cleared,
but also that full route cache,
and we make sure that it's not some pre-rendered page
that's reused over and over again.
Of course, we don't have to use this setting
to make sure that we see updated data.
A different approach would be to revalidate the cache
of a specific page on demand
with the revalidate path function we already used
in the previous section, and that's now a function
which we'll revisit in the next lecture
before we then thereafter will take a look
at how we can manage caching
if we're not sending a request to a separate backend,
but instead to some other data source,
like a database we manage in the NextJS application.

lectures.title: On-Demand Cache Invalidation with revalidatePath & revalidateTag

cues.en: So revalidatePath
is another way of making sure
that cached data is thrown away.
And a key difference compared
to setting dynamic, force dynamic
or using the noStore function
or using the configuration on the fetch function
is that all those settings
either disable caching altogether
or set a certain caching time period.
When calling revalidatePath,
we instead revalidate some piece of the cache
on demand when we tell NextJS to do it.
And that can be more efficient than disabling
the cache forever or setting a timeframe for caching.
Because with that timeframe, we of course would get NextJS
to re-fetch data every five seconds, for example,
which is redundant if the data
didn't change within those five seconds.
So that's a bit inefficient then.
That's the advantage of explicitly telling NextJS
to revalidate the cache, because if we
as a Next developer know that some data changed,
we can simply tell NextJS about that and, therefore,
get the best of both worlds:
as much caching as possible,
but updated data when we need it.
Now, revalidatePath can be configured in different ways,
and you can learn all about that
in the official documentation.
The main idea simply is that you define the path.
So for example, '/messages'
that users might visit on your website,
and all the data related to that path
and the route cache related to that path will be deleted.
What's important to note, though,
is that any nested paths and nested pages
will not have their data and route cache deleted
and revalidated, unless you also specify
a second argument here and set this to 'layout'.
If you do that, you essentially tell NextJS
that it should revalidate this cache for this path
and also revalidate the cache of all nested pages.
If you instead set this setting to 'page'
or omit it, since 'page' is the default,
only the cache of this specific page
will be revalidated and cleared.
Hence, if you would want to clear all the cached data
of all pages of your page, you would have to set the path
to just '/', so to the root path of the application
and add 'layout', and that would now clear the cache data
and the route cache of all pages on your site.
That's how revalidatePath works.
Of course, you can also call it multiple time
if you would want to revalidate the path
of different pages like this.
That would be possible as well.
In addition to revalidatePath,
there also is a revalidateTag function you can call
that's also imported from 'next/cache'.
And revalidateTag then takes a tag like 'msg' as an input.
But how does this function work now?
Well, you can assign tags to requests
that fetch data that will be cached.
For example, here, when sending that fetch request,
I can add that configuration object with that next key.
And then there, besides setting that revalidate option
you saw before, I can set up some tags,
and that will be an array of strings.
And here you can set up any tags you want,
for example, 'msg'.
And you can assign multiple tags
to one request if you want to.
Now, these tags will, under the hood,
be connected to the cached data,
and if you then call revalidateTag with a certain tag,
NextJS will revalidate and throw away
any cached data that has that tag.
So that would allow you to clear the cache
of multiple pages if those different pages
would assign the same tags to their requests.
So instead of calling revalidatePath multiple times
for different pages, you could just use one
and the same tag on different pages
and then just revalidate that tag
to clear all the cached data of those pages.
Now to show you how this works,
I'll call revalidate tag with 'msg' as a tag here
in this new message page component
when that form is submitted.
And I'm not doing anything else
with that submitted data right now,
but we'll change that soon.
I'll comment out this line here
so that I'm not storing anything in the database,
so that I really just use that as a dummy function
right now to show you revalidateTag.
And I did set the same tag here on my messages page.
And with that set up, if I restart
my development server here and I restart the backend server,
you will see that if I reload this messages page
multiple times, I got no logs here,
which hopefully makes sense
because we're caching and reusing data.
But because I assigned that tag and I revalidate that tag
after submitting the forum on the new message page,
if I go to the new message page
and enter some message here, doesn't matter,
we're not using it anyways, and I click send,
you will see that now I got some logs here;
because I revalidated the cached data connected
to my request, to my fetch request here,
and hence it was resent.
And that's the idea behind revalidateTag and revalidatePath.
